metadata.note: The Petersburg Railroad -- chartered by Virginia in early 1830 and completed by August 1833 from Petersburg (on the Appomattox River) south to Blakely, Virginia, just across the Roanoke River from Weldon, North Carolina -- the first railroad in the South built in a north-south direction, and part of the very first generation of American railroads. It ran through Belfield and Hicksford (both merged in 1887 into present-day Emporia, VA). At Weldon it met the Wilmington and Weldon Railroad and the Raleigh and Gaston Railroad, making Weldon a key junction for through traffic between the Northeast and the Deep South for the rest of the 19th century. During the Civil War the line carried food and supplies to Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia at Petersburg; a Union raid destroyed track here on Dec 8 1864, briefly disrupting that supply line (part of the Siege of Petersburg operations sometimes called the Battle of the Weldon Railroad, though that name properly refers to fighting on a different line, the Petersburg & Weldon-adjacent tracks closer to the city). Atlantic Coast Line bought the Petersburg Railroad in 1893, after which it lost its independent identity -- but not its traffic: this is the same physical corridor as the Champion and Florida Special already on this map (see atlantic_coast_line.geojson) and, later, Amtrak's Silver Meteor, Palmetto, and Carolinian (see amtrak.geojson). Unlike most lines on this map, it has never lost passenger service in nearly two centuries. GEOMETRY METHODOLOGY: real-traced through OpenStreetMap active-rail data (Overpass API, shortest-path graph search); traced length 109.8 km / 68.2 mi, passing within 200m of Emporia (the historic Belfield/Hicksford), corroborating the routing.

segments.note: Chartered by Virginia in early 1830, completed Petersburg-Blakely (opposite Weldon, NC across the Roanoke River) by August 1833 -- the first north-south railroad in the South; ran through Belfield and Hicksford (merged 1887 into Emporia, VA); connected at Weldon to the Wilmington and Weldon and the Raleigh and Gaston railroads. Carried Confederate supply traffic to Lee's army at Petersburg during the Civil War until a Dec 8 1864 Union raid briefly cut the line. Frequency estimated, unsourced; bought by the Atlantic Coast Line in 1893, after which it lost its independent identity -- the same corridor continued (and still continues) to carry passenger trains, see atlantic_coast_line.geojson and amtrak.geojson
